script.opening: "My hands have got shaky over the last few years, doctor. It’s worst when I reach for my tea or try to write — my writing’s gone spidery — but when they’re resting in my lap they’re fine. Funny thing, a glass of wine settles it. My dad had the same. I’m really worried it’s the start of Parkinson’s — is it?"

facts.text: About 4 years, slowly worse. Both hands about the same. Worse holding a cup, a newspaper, a spoon, doing up small buttons, writing. Fine with hands resting in his lap. Worse when tired, nervous or after strong coffee. A glass of wine settles it for an hour or so. If asked: his head sometimes nods "no-no" slightly; voice fine.

Hands still when resting on his lap. Shake when held out in front, more when he tries to touch his nose or draw a spiral. Can walk across the room normally with arms swinging, turn easily, and get up from a chair without using his hands.
No slowness, no stiffness, no shuffling, walking normal, no falls. Sense of smell fine. No acting out dreams. Bowels normal. Handwriting is shaky, not small. Face expression normal (his wife says).

No weight loss, no palpitations, not sweaty or hot. Drinks 5–6 mugs of strong tea a day. Alcohol: 2 glasses of wine most evenings — "it helps the shaking at dinner". No new medicines; not on asthma inhalers, lithium, valproate or antidepressants.
High cholesterol (atorvastatin). No asthma, no heart problems, no slow pulse that he knows of. No allergies.

Father had a shaky hand "for years" and lived to 88 — "he never had Parkinson’s, I don’t think". Retired accountant. Married to Moira. Loves eating out with friends, now avoids it because he spills soup and wine. Sings in a choir.

Polite, articulate, quietly very anxious about Parkinson’s — a friend from the choir has it and is "going downhill fast". If the doctor explains the difference clearly, show huge relief. Interested in a tablet "for eating out".

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his choir friend with Parkinson’s; fear of ending up the same. Embarrassment eating out; has started using wine to steady his hands.
ice.expectations: "Tell me whether it’s Parkinson’s, and whether anything helps."

cues: "When they’re resting in my lap they’re fine" — the action-versus-rest distinction.
"A glass of wine settles it" — alcohol response, and a habit to discuss.
"I spill things, I’ve started avoiding going out" — functional impact that guides treatment.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ESSENTIAL TREMOR — action/postural, bilateral/symmetrical, worse with action and better at rest, often familial, alcohol-responsive, no bradykinesia/rigidity/gait change

DISTINGUISHES it from PARKINSON’S (resting, asymmetric, pill-rolling tremor, better with action, WITH bradykinesia, rigidity and gait/postural changes) — using rest-vs-action and the presence/absence of the parkinsonian triad
Screens OTHER/REVERSIBLE causes — enhanced physiological (anxiety/caffeine), hyperthyroidism (TFTs), drugs (salbutamol/lithium/SSRIs — review), alcohol, cerebellar/dystonic tremor

EXAMINES (face to face) for the discriminating features — tremor at rest/posture/action (finger-nose, cup, writing/spiral), bradykinesia (finger-tapping/arm swing), rigidity (cogwheel), gait and cerebellar signs

MANAGES essential tremor — reassurance if mild; PROPRANOLOL (licensed; contraindications checked — asthma, bradycardia/heart block, heart failure) or primidone if functionally impairing/distressing; reduce caffeine, review drugs, treat thyroid — and refers to neurology if uncertain/atypical/parkinsonian/cerebellar/refractory
Directly ADDRESSES the Parkinson’s FEAR — explaining why this looks like essential tremor rather than Parkinson’s — and explores embarrassment/functional impact empathetically
Explains the diagnosis and reasoning in accessible terms and checks understanding, neither over-investigating nor dismissing

Safety-nets and follows up: what would prompt review/referral (asymmetry, slowness/stiffness, gait change, worsening function), treatment trial and review, reversible-cause results, and reassurance — action-vs-rest distinction with the Parkinson’s fear addressed

worked.txt: "Let me reassure you on the big worry first: what you’re describing actually points AWAY from Parkinson’s. Your shake is worst when you USE your hands and settles at rest — Parkinson’s tremor is the opposite, worse at rest — and it’s both sides and runs in your family. That all fits a different, much more benign condition called essential tremor."

"I’d like to check properly in person — hands resting in your lap, then arms out, then reaching to my finger and writing a spiral. I’ll also check for slowness, stiffness and your walking, because those are the things we’d see in Parkinson’s. If none of those are there, that’s reassuring."
"I’ll do a thyroid blood test, because an overactive thyroid can cause a tremor, and review your medicines and caffeine, as those can make any tremor worse."
"So this is essential tremor — common, often inherited, and not Parkinson’s and not dangerous. The classic clue you gave me is that a little alcohol settles it; that’s very typical."

"If it’s mainly a nuisance, we can leave it. But if it’s embarrassing or getting in the way of writing and drinking, there’s a tablet — propranolol — that often helps, as long as you don’t have asthma or certain heart problems, which I’ll check. How much is it bothering you day to day?"

"Come back if it becomes one-sided, you notice slowness or stiffness, your walking changes, or it’s affecting you more — then I’d involve a neurologist. Otherwise we can trial treatment and review. Does that ease your mind a bit?"

f.learning: Distinguish ESSENTIAL TREMOR from PARKINSON’S — the core skill in a "shaking hands" presentation. Essential tremor is a postural/action/kinetic tremor that is WORSE ON ACTION and posture (reaching, holding, writing — spidery, eating) and BETTER at rest, typically BILATERAL and fairly SYMMETRICAL, often FAMILIAL, frequently IMPROVED by a small amount of alcohol, sometimes with head ("yes-yes"/"no-no") or voice tremor, and crucially WITHOUT bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance. Parkinson’s tremor, by contrast, is a RESTING "pill-rolling" tremor, typically ASYMMETRIC (one side first), BETTER with action, and accompanied by the parkinsonian features — BRADYKINESIA (slowness, reduced arm swing, micrographia that decrements), RIGIDITY (cogwheel) and gait/postural changes (shuffling, stooped, festination) — so the rest-vs-action distinction and the presence/absence of the parkinsonian triad are the discriminators. Consider other tremors: enhanced PHYSIOLOGICAL (anxiety, caffeine, fatigue), HYPERTHYROIDISM (check TFTs), DRUGS (salbutamol, lithium, SSRIs, valproate — review), excess alcohol/withdrawal, cerebellar INTENTION tremor (worse approaching a target, with cerebellar signs) and dystonic tremor. Examine the tremor at rest, on posture (arms outstretched) and on action (finger-nose, cup, writing/spiral), and assess for bradykinesia, rigidity, gait and cerebellar signs, which underpins the diagnosis and reassurance. Manage essential tremor by reassuring when mild (directly addressing the Parkinson’s fear), and offering PROPRANOLOL (licensed for essential tremor; check for asthma, bradycardia/heart block and heart failure first) or primidone when functionally impairing or socially distressing (BNF; clinical practice rather than a guideline recommendation), while reducing caffeine, reviewing aggravating drugs and treating thyroid abnormality; refer to neurology for diagnostic uncertainty, atypical/asymmetric features, suspected parkinsonism (NICE NG71: quickly and untreated) or cerebellar signs, or refractory tremor. The hidden agenda is fear of Parkinson’s plus embarrassment/functional impact; make the action-vs-rest distinction, reassure appropriately while screening properly, address the impact and offer treatment, and refer if uncertain.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG71 (Parkinson’s disease in adults, 2017) · [2] BNF propranolol and primidone monographs · [3] Consensus statement on the classification of tremors (International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society, 2018) (international) · [4] NICE NG145 (thyroid disease: assessment and management, 2019) · [5] NICE HTG474 (unilateral MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy for treatment-resistant essential tremor; formerly IPG617)
knowledge.summary: A slowly progressive, bilateral, fairly symmetrical action and postural tremor of the hands, eased by alcohol, with a father affected and no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait change, is essential tremor. Examine to prove the absence of parkinsonism, screen thyroid function and drugs, answer the Parkinson’s fear directly, and offer treatment only if the tremor limits him.

points.t: A bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for at least 3 years, with or without tremor of the head, voice or legs, and without other neurological signs such as dystonia, ataxia or parkinsonism [3]. Often familial and often eased by a little alcohol.

NICE NG71 [1]: diagnose clinically using the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria, in which bradykinesia is required, with rest tremor, rigidity or postural instability. The tremor is typically at rest, asymmetric at onset and eases on movement. Refer suspected Parkinson’s quickly and untreated to a specialist with expertise in its diagnosis and management [1].

Watch the hands at rest in the lap, with arms outstretched, and in action (finger–nose, pouring, drawing a spiral, writing). Test repetitive finger taps for slowing and shrinking amplitude, tone at the wrist for cogwheeling, arm swing and gait. Look for cerebellar signs (intention tremor, past-pointing) and dystonic postures.

Enhanced physiological tremor (anxiety, caffeine, fatigue), hyperthyroidism (check TFTs, NICE NG145 [4]), drugs (beta-agonists, lithium, SSRIs, valproate, amiodarone, steroids), alcohol withdrawal, cerebellar and dystonic tremor.

Reassurance is enough if the tremor does not limit him. If it affects function or causes distress, propranolol is licensed for essential tremor and primidone is an alternative (BNF [2]); start low and titrate, dose per BNF. Check for asthma, heart block, bradycardia and heart failure before propranolol.

Neurology if the diagnosis is uncertain, features are asymmetric or atypical, parkinsonian or cerebellar signs are present, or the tremor is disabling despite treatment. Specialist options include deep brain stimulation and focused ultrasound thalamotomy under special arrangements (NICE HTG474 [5]).
Some people report brief improvement with alcohol, but it is neither a diagnostic test nor a treatment. Using drink to steady the hands risks dependence and rebound tremor.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Caffeine; alcohol not to be used as treatment; drug review; thyroid treated if abnormal.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

ro.d: Picked up the Parkinson’s fear, the social embarrassment and the alcohol clue, and explored drinking without judgement.
Idea: shaking means Parkinson’s. Concern: Parkinson’s and embarrassment. Expectation: an answer and help.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his choir friend with Parkinson’s; fear of ending up the same. Embarrassment eating out; has started using wine to steady his hands — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Brankin, I’m Dr Osei. What brings you in today?

My hands have got shaky over the last few years. It’s worst when I reach for my tea or write — my writing’s gone spidery — but resting in my lap they’re fine. Funny thing, a glass of wine settles it. My dad had the same. I’m really worried it’s the start of Parkinson’s. Is it?
That’s a very clear description, and I can hear the worry. I want to answer that question properly, so can I ask a few things and examine you, and then tell you what I think?
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and promises to answer it after assessment

model.text: Yes, please.
Is it both hands, and roughly equal? Has it ever affected your head nodding, or your voice?
Both hands, about the same. Just my hands, I think.
Have you noticed yourself slowing down — buttons, turning over in bed, your walking getting shuffly, or people saying your arm doesn’t swing? Any stiffness?
model.why: Screens for bradykinesia, rigidity and gait change

model.text: No, none of that. My walking’s fine.
Any change in your sense of smell, acting out dreams in your sleep, constipation, or dizziness when you stand?
Not that I’ve noticed.

Other things can make a tremor worse. How much tea and coffee do you have? Any weight loss, feeling hot, or racing heart? I’ll also go through your repeat list with you for any medicine that can cause shaking.
model.why: Screens caffeine, thyroid features and drug causes

model.text: I’ve not really counted the cups. No weight loss that I know of.
You said a glass of wine settles it. How much do you drink in a usual week? Some people find they start having a drink just to steady their hands.
Not a lot, I don’t think. But I can see how that could happen.
What makes you think Parkinson’s in particular?
model.why: Explores the idea behind the fear

model.text: Everyone says shaking hands means Parkinson’s. And going out for a meal, I spill things. I’ve started avoiding it.
That sounds embarrassing and it’s affecting what you enjoy. What were you hoping I could do today?
model.why: Acknowledges social impact and elicits expectations

model.text: Tell me whether it is Parkinson’s. And whether anything helps.
Rest your hands in your lap, and count backwards from 20 for me. … Now arms out in front. … Now touch my finger then your nose. Could you draw a spiral here, and pour this cup of water into that one?
model.why: Examines tremor at rest, on posture and in action

model.text: (The hands are still at rest, shake with arms outstretched and while drawing.)
Now tap your finger and thumb together, big and fast, as long as you can. … Let me feel your wrists while you move the other hand. … And walk to the door and back for me.
model.why: Tests for bradykinesia, rigidity and gait

model.text: How was that?

The good news first. Your tremor comes on with holding and using your hands and settles at rest. Your finger taps stay fast and big, there’s no stiffness, and your walking and arm swing are normal. That pattern is essential tremor, not Parkinson’s.
model.why: Answers the question directly with the reasons

model.text: So I haven’t got Parkinson’s?

From everything I’ve seen, no. Parkinson’s tremor is usually at rest, starts on one side, and comes with slowness and stiffness — you have none of those. Essential tremor often runs in families, like your dad, and alcohol easing it is typical. It can slowly get a bit more noticeable over the years, but it doesn’t turn into Parkinson’s.
model.why: Explains the rest versus action distinction in plain words

model.text: That’s a huge relief.

I’d like a blood test for your thyroid, as an overactive thyroid can cause a shake, and I’ll check your pulse and blood pressure now. Cutting down on tea may help a little. Wine does steady it, but I’d rather you didn’t use a drink before going out — it can creep up, and the shake can be worse the next day.
model.why: TFTs, caffeine advice and caution about self-medicating with alcohol

model.text: Fair enough. Is there a tablet?

There is. Propranolol helps many people. Do you have asthma, or any heart problems? … If it doesn’t suit you, there’s an alternative called primidone. There’s no need to take anything if it isn’t bothering you enough — it’s your choice.
model.why: Offers propranolol after checking contraindications; primidone alternative; shared decision

model.text: I think I’d like to try it, for eating out.

Then we’ll start at a low dose and review. Some practical things help too — a heavier mug, a cup with a lid, holding it with both hands. If things change, or treatment doesn’t help enough, I’ll refer you to neurology.
Please come back sooner if you notice slowness, stiffness, the shake appearing at rest or on one side, a change in walking, or falls. Can you tell me what you’ll take home from today?
It’s essential tremor, not Parkinson’s. Thyroid test, less tea, not using wine for it, try the tablet, and come back if I slow down or it changes.
Perfect. I’ll see you in about a month with the blood result to see how the propranolol is going.

social.t: Spilling in public causes embarrassment and withdrawal. Practical aids — weighted cutlery, lidded cups, two-handed holding — and occupational therapy help.
Some people find alcohol briefly steadies the tremor; it is not a diagnostic test, but asking about it opens a non-judgemental conversation about drinking.

legal.t: Drivers must tell the DVLA about any condition that affects safe driving. Ask whether the tremor affects his control of a vehicle; if it does, advise him to check the DVLA guidance and record the advice.

professional.t: If Parkinson’s is suspected, NICE NG71 advises quick referral to a specialist before any treatment starts.
Treatment is optional; offer it and respect his choice (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: National Tremor Foundation for patient information and support groups; occupational therapy for adaptive equipment.

redFlags: Rest tremor, one-sided onset, slowness, stiffness, shuffling gait or falls — suspected Parkinson’s, refer untreated (NICE NG71)
Cerebellar signs — intention tremor, ataxia, slurred speech
psychosocial: Alcohol used to steady the hands
ice: Expectation: a clear answer and help

playbook.diagnosis: Essential tremor: bilateral, symmetrical action and postural hand tremor for several years, alcohol-responsive, familial, with no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait change on examination. Thyroid and drug causes to be excluded.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s called essential tremor. It shows when you use or hold your hands, runs in families and isn’t Parkinson’s. It doesn’t turn into Parkinson’s, and there are treatments if it bothers you.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was Parkinson’s, like many people would be. Your examination doesn’t show Parkinson’s — here’s what I found.”
management.psychosocial: Address embarrassment and eating-out avoidance; discourage using alcohol as treatment.
sharedPlan: Propranolol if he wishes, after checking for asthma, bradycardia, heart block and heart failure; primidone as alternative; dose per BNF
Practical aids; occupational therapy if needed
Neurology if uncertain, atypical or refractory
safetyNet: Return sooner for slowness, stiffness, rest or one-sided tremor, gait change or falls
Review in about a month with TFT result and treatment response

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards a candidate who examines to prove what it is not. Reassurance without examination, or a referral that ignores his question, both miss the point.

items.fail: Reassuring without examining for bradykinesia and rigidity.
items.why: The absence of parkinsonian signs is the basis of the diagnosis.
items.fix: Examine rest, posture and action tremor, finger taps, tone and gait.

items.fail: Forgetting thyroid function and the drug list.
items.why: Hyperthyroidism and drugs are reversible causes.

items.fail: Prescribing propranolol without asking about asthma or heart problems.
items.why: It is contraindicated in asthma and some heart conditions (BNF).
items.fix: Ask, check pulse and BP, then start low.
Answer it directly and explain the reasons.

items.fail: Ignoring the embarrassment and the alcohol clue.
items.why: These are the cues to impact and to a possible risk.
items.fix: Explore avoidance and gently discourage alcohol as treatment.

items.fail: No clear reason to come back.
items.why: Parkinson’s can emerge later; he needs to recognise it.
items.fix: Name slowness, stiffness, rest or one-sided tremor, gait change and falls.

Sites, symmetry, bradykinesia, gait, non-motor features, caffeine, thyroid, drugs, alcohol.
Why Parkinson’s; embarrassment when eating out; what he wants.
Rest, posture and action; spiral and pouring; finger taps, tone, gait and arm swing.
Essential tremor, not Parkinson’s; TFTs; caffeine; alcohol caution; propranolol or primidone if wanted; practical aids.

wordPics.fail: Says “it’s probably nothing” without examining; or starts Parkinson’s medication; misses the drug and thyroid screen; prescribes propranolol without asking about asthma; ignores the embarrassment.
wordPics.pass: Distinguishes action from rest tremor; examines for bradykinesia and rigidity; checks TFTs and drugs; reassures that it is essential tremor; offers propranolol if troublesome.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: answers the Parkinson’s question directly with the reasons; explores the social avoidance; gently addresses using alcohol to self-treat; checks contraindications; lets him choose; practical aids; clear return criteria; he leaves relieved and with a plan.

avoid.dont: “Let’s not worry about Parkinson’s for now.”
avoid.instead: “You asked if it’s Parkinson’s — from what I’ve found, it isn’t, and here’s why.”
avoid.why: Leaving the stated fear unanswered loses Relating to Others marks.

avoid.dont: “Well, if wine helps, a drink before a meal out is fine.”
avoid.instead: “Wine does steady it, but I’d rather we used something safer.”
avoid.why: Alcohol as self-treatment risks dependence and rebound tremor.

avoid.instead: “Before this tablet, do you have asthma or any heart problems?”
avoid.why: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma and some heart conditions (BNF).

Perfect. I’ll see you in about a month with the blood result to see how the propranolol is going.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG71 (Parkinson’s disease in adults, 2017) · [2] BNF propranolol and primidone monographs · [3] Consensus statement on the classification of tremors (International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society, 2018) (international) · [4] NICE NG145 (thyroid disease: assessment and management, 2019) · [5] NICE HTG474 (unilateral MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy for treatment-resistant essential tremor; formerly IPG617)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A slowly progressive, bilateral, fairly symmetrical action and postural tremor of the hands, eased by alcohol, with a father affected and no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait change, is essential tremor. Examine to prove the absence of parkinsonism, screen thyroid function and drugs, answer the Parkinson’s fear directly, and offer treatment only if the tremor limits him.

points.t: A bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for at least 3 years, with or without tremor of the head, voice or legs, and without other neurological signs such as dystonia, ataxia or parkinsonism [3]. Often familial and often eased by a little alcohol.

NICE NG71 [1]: diagnose clinically using the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria, in which bradykinesia is required, with rest tremor, rigidity or postural instability. The tremor is typically at rest, asymmetric at onset and eases on movement. Refer suspected Parkinson’s quickly and untreated to a specialist with expertise in its diagnosis and management [1].

Watch the hands at rest in the lap, with arms outstretched, and in action (finger–nose, pouring, drawing a spiral, writing). Test repetitive finger taps for slowing and shrinking amplitude, tone at the wrist for cogwheeling, arm swing and gait. Look for cerebellar signs (intention tremor, past-pointing) and dystonic postures.

Enhanced physiological tremor (anxiety, caffeine, fatigue), hyperthyroidism (check TFTs, NICE NG145 [4]), drugs (beta-agonists, lithium, SSRIs, valproate, amiodarone, steroids), alcohol withdrawal, cerebellar and dystonic tremor.

Reassurance is enough if the tremor does not limit him. If it affects function or causes distress, propranolol is licensed for essential tremor and primidone is an alternative (BNF [2]); start low and titrate, dose per BNF. Check for asthma, heart block, bradycardia and heart failure before propranolol.

Neurology if the diagnosis is uncertain, features are asymmetric or atypical, parkinsonian or cerebellar signs are present, or the tremor is disabling despite treatment. Specialist options include deep brain stimulation and focused ultrasound thalamotomy under special arrangements (NICE HTG474 [5]).
Some people report brief improvement with alcohol, but it is neither a diagnostic test nor a treatment. Using drink to steady the hands risks dependence and rebound tremor.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the tremor, the alcohol effect, his father and his fear before narrowing.
Asked about eating out, spilling, avoidance, caffeine and alcohol use.
Picked up the Parkinson’s fear, the social embarrassment and the alcohol clue, and explored drinking without judgement.
Idea: shaking means Parkinson’s. Concern: Parkinson’s and embarrassment. Expectation: an answer and help.
Examined rest, posture and action tremor, finger taps, tone, gait and arm swing; TFTs; pulse and BP before propranolol.
Essential tremor versus Parkinson’s, enhanced physiological, thyroid, drug-induced, cerebellar and dystonic tremor.
Screened bradykinesia, rigidity, gait change and non-motor features; thyroid features; drug review.
Essential tremor explained with the reasons it is not Parkinson’s.
Reassurance plus propranolol after checking asthma and heart contraindications, primidone as alternative; practical aids; his choice.
Caffeine; alcohol not to be used as treatment; drug review; thyroid treated if abnormal.
Return for slowness, stiffness, rest or one-sided tremor, gait change or falls; review in a month; neurology if uncertain or refractory.

social.t: Spilling in public causes embarrassment and withdrawal. Practical aids — weighted cutlery, lidded cups, two-handed holding — and occupational therapy help.
Some people find alcohol briefly steadies the tremor; it is not a diagnostic test, but asking about it opens a non-judgemental conversation about drinking.

legal.t: Drivers must tell the DVLA about any condition that affects safe driving. Ask whether the tremor affects his control of a vehicle; if it does, advise him to check the DVLA guidance and record the advice.

professional.t: If Parkinson’s is suspected, NICE NG71 advises quick referral to a specialist before any treatment starts.
Treatment is optional; offer it and respect his choice (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: National Tremor Foundation for patient information and support groups; occupational therapy for adaptive equipment.

redFlags: Rest tremor, one-sided onset, slowness, stiffness, shuffling gait or falls — suspected Parkinson’s, refer untreated (NICE NG71)
Cerebellar signs — intention tremor, ataxia, slurred speech
psychosocial: Alcohol used to steady the hands
ice: Expectation: a clear answer and help

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Essential tremor: bilateral, symmetrical action and postural hand tremor for several years, alcohol-responsive, familial, with no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait change on examination. Thyroid and drug causes to be excluded.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s called essential tremor. It shows when you use or hold your hands, runs in families and isn’t Parkinson’s. It doesn’t turn into Parkinson’s, and there are treatments if it bothers you.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was Parkinson’s, like many people would be. Your examination doesn’t show Parkinson’s — here’s what I found.”
management.psychosocial: Address embarrassment and eating-out avoidance; discourage using alcohol as treatment.

Practical aids; occupational therapy if needed
Neurology if uncertain, atypical or refractory

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards a candidate who examines to prove what it is not. Reassurance without examination, or a referral that ignores his question, both miss the point.

items.fail: Reassuring without examining for bradykinesia and rigidity.
items.why: The absence of parkinsonian signs is the basis of the diagnosis.
items.fix: Examine rest, posture and action tremor, finger taps, tone and gait.

items.fail: Forgetting thyroid function and the drug list.
items.why: Hyperthyroidism and drugs are reversible causes.

items.fail: Prescribing propranolol without asking about asthma or heart problems.
items.why: It is contraindicated in asthma and some heart conditions (BNF).
items.fix: Ask, check pulse and BP, then start low.
Answer it directly and explain the reasons.

items.fail: Ignoring the embarrassment and the alcohol clue.
items.why: These are the cues to impact and to a possible risk.
items.fix: Explore avoidance and gently discourage alcohol as treatment.

items.fail: No clear reason to come back.
items.why: Parkinson’s can emerge later; he needs to recognise it.
items.fix: Name slowness, stiffness, rest or one-sided tremor, gait change and falls.
